overviews: This paper investigates adaptive event-triggered control for interval type-2 fuzzy cyber-physical systems subject to deception attacks and actuator failures. A membership-function-derivative-dependent switching design and a looped-functional approach are developed for controller synthesis, and two examples are presented. The topic is relevant to secure networked control. The following minor points should be addressed to improve the presentation of the manuscript.

This manuscript considers the joint design of fuzzy controllers and an adaptive event-triggering mechanism for cyber-physical systems with deception attacks and Markov-type actuator failures. The analysis uses membership-function derivative information and a two-sided looped functional to obtain LMI-based design conditions. The problem is of interest. Some explanations of the design methodology could be improved, as detailed below.

The paper studies adaptive event-triggered control of interval type-2 fuzzy systems under cyberattacks and actuator failures. The proposed design is illustrated by a PMSM example and a numerical example. The manuscript would benefit from clearer discussion of the simulation results and the scope of the conclusions. My specific comments are as follows.
comments: The manuscript requires careful editing to improve English grammar and sentence structure. Some sentences are overly complex or awkwardly phrased, which may hinder comprehension for international readers. Professional language polishing is recommended.

The practical motivation could be made more concrete. Please explain how deception attacks, actuator failures, and limited communication resources arise together in the application considered, and relate this discussion to the PMSM example.

The meaning of certain design parameters is not sufficiently explained. In particular, please clarify the roles of ξ_1 and ξ_2 in Theorem 3.2 so that readers can better understand the controller synthesis conditions.
The manuscript contains some minor typesetting errors. For example, the Introduction contains a duplicated full stop after "CPSs". A careful proofreading is recommended to correct such errors.

The terminology in the simulation figures should be checked. In Figs. 7 and 13, the vertical-axis label "Operation models" should be revised to "Operating modes" to agree with the actuator-failure description in the text.

The literature discussion could be strengthened by including additional recent studies on secure event-triggered control of interval type-2 fuzzy systems. Their connections with the present work should also be briefly discussed.

The manuscript needs further editing for technical English, particularly in the Abstract and the description of the control design. Please improve the grammar and sentence structure so that the objectives and results can be followed more easily.

Two-sided looped functionals have been used in related studies. Please expand Remark 3.1 to explain the rationale for the functional selected here, especially how the membership information and the information within a sampling interval are incorporated.

The closed-loop model includes both deception attacks and actuator failures, which makes its presentation somewhat involved. A short explanatory paragraph after Eq. (15), distinguishing how these two effects enter the feedback path, would help readers follow the model.

The controller synthesis procedure could be described in greater detail. Please summarize the main offline design steps, from specifying the parameters and solving the LMIs to obtaining the controller gains and the event-triggering weighting matrix.

The discussion of the adaptive triggering mechanism could be improved. Please clarify its distinction from a fixed-threshold mechanism and explain how the threshold update in Eq. (6) affects the triggering condition in Eq. (5).

Some recent developments closely related to adaptive event-triggered and secure fuzzy control could be added to the Introduction. A concise discussion would help place the proposed design in the context of existing research.

The English expression should be improved throughout the manuscript. In particular, some sentences in the Abstract and Conclusion are lengthy, and a more concise presentation would make the main results clearer.

In Table 1, the number of transmitted packets increases as σ increases. A more detailed explanation of this observation, with reference to the adaptive threshold, would improve the discussion of the numerical results.

The communication saving rate should be defined explicitly. Please explain how it is calculated from the reported transmission counts in Table 1 and Example 2, and check the numerical percentages for consistency.

The discussion of Fig. 12 could be expanded. Please explain what the control-input curve and the membership-function-derivative curve illustrate in the proposed scheme, and relate their evolution to the closed-loop responses.
The Conclusion already mentions possible extensions. It would be helpful to state the scope of the present state-feedback formulation more clearly before discussing these future directions.

The Introduction would benefit from a few additional recent references on event-triggered control of interval type-2 fuzzy systems under deception attacks. Please explain their relevance to the problem studied in this paper.
responses: We have revised the Abstract and the first paragraph of the Conclusion to shorten long sentences and make the description of the method more direct. We also edited the Introduction and the model description for grammar and terminology. For example, "the transmitted data is" has been corrected to "the transmitted data are", "where K_n denote" to "where K_n denotes", and "condition ... guarantee" to "condition ... guarantees". The manuscript now describes fixed thresholds as not adjusting online, without implying that all fixed-threshold schemes perform poorly under disturbances.

We have added a paragraph connecting the problem formulation to the PMSM example. It explains that the attack model affects transmitted current and angular-velocity measurements, the actuator-failure model reduces the effective control input, and the trigger limits data transmissions. This connects the three modeled effects to data integrity, actuator reliability, and communication efficiency in a networked motor drive. The example is presented as an engineering illustration of the joint setting; no field measurements or new experimental observations are claimed.

We have added an explanation immediately before Theorem 3.2. The scalars ξ_1 and ξ_2 are prescribed synthesis parameters specifying the proportionality relations Q_2 = ξ_1 Q_1 and Q_3 = ξ_2 Q_1 used in the variable transformation. They are held fixed during each LMI feasibility solve, and different choices may affect feasibility. The new text also distinguishes these scalars from physical plant or attack parameters. The parameter values used in the examples have not been changed.

The duplicated full stop after "CPSs" has been removed from the Introduction. We also checked the edited passages for punctuation and corrected the grammatical inconsistencies described in Response 1. The displayed mathematical expressions have been retained as in the original manuscript.

We have corrected the vertical-axis label from "Operation models" to "Operating modes" in both Figs. 7 and 13. The terminology now agrees with the description of the actuator-failure modes. Their captions have also been shortened to "Actuator-failure mode r(t)" for clearer layout. Within the figures, only the axis-title text was replaced; the switching traces, axis ticks, time interval, and reported results are unchanged.

We have added two recent studies as References [34] and [35] and cited both in a new paragraph in the Introduction. Reference [34] concerns torus-event-based sliding-mode control under deception attacks, while [35] studies adaptive event-triggered asynchronous control of uncertain IT-2 fuzzy Markov jump systems. The paragraph relates these studies to communication scheduling and secure fuzzy control, then states the continuous-time model and membership-function-derivative-based focus of the present paper. The bibliographic details were checked against the publisher records.

We have edited the Abstract, Introduction, model description, and Conclusion for grammar, sentence length, and terminology. The Abstract now states the modeling components, use of membership-function derivative information, joint controller/triggering-matrix design, and simulation examples in shorter sentences. We also corrected subject-verb agreement in the transmitted-data and controller-gain descriptions and in the proof text. These are presentation edits and do not change the displayed mathematical statements.

We have expanded Remark 3.1 to explain the components of the existing functional. The added text describes how the FMF-weighted matrices retain membership dependence, how the elapsed and remaining sampling-interval distances enter the construction, and how the two integrals in V_3 use derivative information on either side of the current time. It also explains the augmented-vector terms in V_2 and V_4 and the threshold term V_5. This addition explains the construction directly; it does not introduce an untested quantitative claim of superiority over other functionals.

We have added a paragraph immediately after Eq. (15). It explains that the Bernoulli variable selects whether the controller receives the transmitted state or the deception signal, whereas the actuator-effectiveness matrix changes the input delivered to the plant. This distinguishes an effect on the information used by the controller from an effect on the applied control input. The paragraph points back to the two corresponding terms in the closed-loop model.

We have added an offline synthesis paragraph at the end of Section 3. It first identifies the model data and scalars to be fixed, then directs the reader to the feasibility conditions in Theorem 3.3, including the stated Markov modes, fuzzy-rule pairs, and applicable sign conditions. It gives the recovery expressions for the controller gains and triggering matrix. The triggering-matrix expression follows from the congruence transformation in the proof of Theorem 3.2. Finally, the paragraph clarifies that infeasibility for a selected parameter choice does not by itself prove that no stabilizing controller exists.

We have expanded Remark 2.2 with a direct comparison. A fixed-threshold trigger leaves its threshold constant. Under Eq. (6), for a positive threshold and nonzero triggering error, the threshold increases below 1/σ and decreases above 1/σ; the update is zero when the error is zero or the threshold equals 1/σ. The added text then explains that, for fixed state, error, and weighting matrix, a larger threshold makes Eq. (5) harder to satisfy. We also revised the description of σ below Eq. (6) to state its equilibrium-setting role. The discussion does not assume a universal reduction in transmissions relative to every fixed-threshold scheme.

We have added two recent studies as References [34] and [35] and cited both in a new paragraph in the Introduction. Reference [34] concerns torus-event-based sliding-mode control under deception attacks, while [35] studies adaptive event-triggered asynchronous control of uncertain IT-2 fuzzy Markov jump systems. The paragraph relates these studies to communication scheduling and secure fuzzy control, then states the continuous-time model and membership-function-derivative-based focus of the present paper. The bibliographic details were checked against the publisher records.

We have rewritten the Abstract and the first paragraph of the Conclusion in shorter sentences and polished the main text for grammar and consistent terminology. The revised Abstract introduces the modeling assumptions and design ingredients in sequence, while the Conclusion states the main results more concisely. We have also revised the final conclusion paragraph as described in Response 5, so the present scope and future directions are easier to distinguish.

We have expanded the paragraph before Table 1. In the reported simulations, increasing σ from 4 to 20 increases the transmitted packet count from 85 to 164, while the equilibrium threshold 1/σ decreases from 0.25 to 0.05. For fixed sampled state, error, and weighting matrix, a smaller threshold makes the triggering condition easier to satisfy. The added explanation also states that the actual count depends on the closed-loop trajectory and threshold evolution. Thus, the discussion explains the observed counts without claiming that the table measures a separate control-performance trade-off.

We have defined the saving rate as (1 − event-triggered count / time-triggered count) × 100%, using counts over the same reported simulation interval. We added the first-row calculation, (1 − 85/400) × 100% = 78.75%, and checked all four rows: 78.75%, 71.75%, 66.00%, and 59.00%. For Example 2, the reported 65 transmissions out of 400 candidates give 83.75%; the previous value of 83.79% has been corrected. The transmission counts are unchanged. This correction is an arithmetic check of the reported counts, not a claim that new simulations were run.

We have expanded the discussion and caption of Fig. 12. The blue curve is identified as the control input and the black curve as the membership-function derivative. The text explains that the input shows the actuation generated by the feedback law, while the derivative sign provides the regional switching information described in Remark 2.4. Both curves approach zero as the states settle. We also clarify that the two quantities are shown together to relate control action and membership dynamics, rather than to compare their magnitudes as a common performance measure.

We have revised the final paragraph of the Conclusion to state the present scope before the future directions. The current formulation uses state feedback, a specified deception-signal bound, and known Markov transition rates. We then retain and sharpen the previously mentioned extensions: observer-based output feedback when full state measurements are unavailable, DoS attacks, and partially unknown transition rates. The revision clarifies the scope of the reported results without presenting these extensions as completed work.

We have added two recent studies as References [34] and [35] and cited both in a new paragraph in the Introduction. Reference [34] concerns torus-event-based sliding-mode control under deception attacks, while [35] studies adaptive event-triggered asynchronous control of uncertain IT-2 fuzzy Markov jump systems. The paragraph relates these studies to communication scheduling and secure fuzzy control, then states the continuous-time model and membership-function-derivative-based focus of the present paper. The bibliographic details were checked against the publisher records.
